Chapter 4: The Realities of Health, Medicine, and Survival
Imagine waking up every morning in fourteenth-century England, knowing that simply staying alive is a victory in itself. Sickness and injury are just part of daily life, lurking around every corner, while the ways to fight them... well, they’re pretty limited. Most folks know pain and hunger up close, and it’s impossible to ignore just how fragile the human body really is. Life tends to be short, and death? It’s never far away.
When it comes to medicine, the knowledge people rely on is this complicated mix of ancient ideas, old wives’ tales, and a touch of practical know-how. University-trained physicians lean heavily on what Galen and Hippocrates taught centuries earlier. They’re obsessed with balancing the four humors—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile. Diagnosis might mean peering into someone’s urine, feeling their pulse, or even asking about their dreams. Treatments range from herbal teas to bloodletting, and the results are... well, let’s just say, they’re hit or miss.
But honestly, most people will never meet a real physician. These doctors are expensive, and the nearest one might be a two-day walk away. So, instead, folks turn to their local healers—midwives, wise women, and neighbors who know a thing or two. Their tools? Herbs, poultices, and prayers handed down through generations. Sometimes these home remedies help. Other times, not so much. Picture a mother, desperate to break her child’s fever—she’ll try willow bark for aches, honey to soothe wounds, maybe even a whispered charm for a bit of luck.
Now, hospitals do exist, but they’re not what you might picture. They’re run by religious orders, more like places of charity than centers of medicine. The sick and poor come for food, shelter, and spiritual comfort. Actual medical care is pretty basic, and the focus is just as much about saving souls as saving bodies. If you’re wealthy, you’ll probably recover at home, surrounded by doctors and servants.
Cleanliness is always a challenge. Water comes from wells or streams, and waste—well, it often ends up in the street or the river. Bathing is rare, especially for the poor, so lice and fleas are regular visitors. The smell of unwashed bodies, animals, and garbage is part of everyday life. Still, people do what they can: scrubbing their hands, changing linens, burning herbs to keep the worst of the odors at bay.
And then, there are the epidemics—the stuff of nightmares. Take the Black Death in the 1340s. It sweeps through England, wiping out a third of the population almost overnight. Its arrival is sudden, terrifying, and completely overwhelming. People die within days, covered in swellings and blackened skin. Fear spreads even faster than the disease. Families abandon loved ones, priests refuse last rites, and some villages end up completely deserted. The memory of that plague sticks with people for generations, shaping how they think about health, fate, and survival itself.
Injuries are everywhere—especially for those working the land or heading off to war. Broken bones, infected wounds, and chronic pain are just facts of life. There are no antibiotics, no real surgery, and nobody understands germs. If you get hurt, it’s all about luck, your own toughness, and support from family and neighbors.
Childbirth is another huge risk. Many women don’t survive labor, and lots of babies never make it past their first days. A midwife, experienced but limited by the tools of her time, does her best to help both mother and child. When things go well, it’s a cause for celebration. When they don’t, loss is deeply felt—but sadly, not unexpected.
Even with all these dangers, people find ways to adapt. They develop a stoic kind of acceptance, leaning on faith, family, and their communities for comfort. There’s laughter, music, and storytelling to ease the hard times. Through it all, the daily fight to survive shapes who they are—building resilience, and helping them treasure the little joys life has to offer.
